headline: A cruise ship people lived on stops in Cambodia

sources.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs (BBC)
They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia. (NBC News)
Residential world cruise suddenly suspends operations, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia (The Independent)

chunks.text: A cruise ship meant to sail around the world for years has stopped in Cambodia, in Southeast Asia. On this [[residential cruise]], people buy or rent a [[cabin]] and live there [[full time]]. The ship {{set out}} from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024. On October 26, 2026, everyone living on the ship had to {{get off}}. The next day, the Florida company that runs it said it [[suspended]] its trips, or stopped them for now.

verbs.wrong: To fix a ship before a trip
verbs.why: Hikers set out early to avoid the heat. Many families set out on long road trips every summer. The ship set out from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024.

verbs.correct: To leave a ship or other vehicle
verbs.wrong: To book a trip months ahead
verbs.why: We get off the bus at the next stop. Passengers get off the plane through the front door. Everyone living on the cruise ship had to get off in Cambodia.

chunks.text: [[Repairs]] {{held up}} the ship's [[departure]] by about four months. The plan was to visit nearly 150 countries over three and a half years. [[Permanent]] cabins cost from 120,000 to 440,000 dollars, and [[rentals]] started at 3,500 dollars a month. People could also {{sign up}} for a [[lifetime plan]] to spend their [[retirement]] at sea. Many residents {{gave up}} their homes on land, and some sold their houses.

verbs.wrong: To cover the cost of repairs
verbs.why: Bad weather often holds up flights in winter. Road work holds up traffic on my street every morning. Repairs held up the ship's departure by about four months.

verbs.correct: To join a plan or program
verbs.why: Many people sign up for a gym plan in January. My parents sign up for a cooking class every fall. People could sign up for a lifetime plan to spend their retirement at sea.

verbs.wrong: To rent a home to someone else
verbs.why: Some students give up their apartments for the summer. People often give up their cars when they move to a big city. Many residents gave up their homes on land to live on the ship.

chunks.text: The company says fuel costs {{went up}} [[sharply]]. Fuel for each cabin used to cost about 1,800 dollars a month. In parts of Asia, it now costs 6,000 to 8,000 dollars. The company tried to {{cut back on}} fuel by sailing more slowly and staying longer in [[ports]]. Those steps {{turned out}} to be too small to {{make up for}} the higher costs. It said it could not {{pass on}} the whole [[increase]] to residents.

verbs.wrong: To change from week to week
verbs.why: Prices go up every winter. Rent goes up almost every year in big cities. The company says fuel costs went up sharply.
My family cuts back on meat to save money. Many drivers cut back on gas when prices are high. The company tried to cut back on fuel by sailing more slowly.

verbs.correct: To be shown to be, in the end
verbs.wrong: To be planned from the start
verbs.why: Some easy jobs turn out to be very hard. Cheap shoes often turn out to be a bad deal. The company's steps turned out to be too small.

verbs.correct: To do enough to balance a loss
verbs.wrong: To hide the real size of a cost
verbs.why: Good tips make up for his low pay. Extra work on Saturday makes up for the hours she misses. Saving fuel was not enough to make up for the higher costs.

verbs.correct: To make someone else pay a cost
verbs.wrong: To split a cost into small parts
verbs.why: Many stores pass on higher costs to shoppers. Airlines pass on fuel costs to travelers through higher fares. The company said it could not pass on the whole increase to residents.

chunks.text: At about 7 a.m., residents {{found out}} from a note that they had to leave by 2 p.m. They had about seven hours to {{move out}} of their cabins. Reports say about 200 people were living [[on board]]. Now many must {{figure out}} where to live. [[Crew members]] are staying to keep the ship in [[good condition]]. The company will spend 60 days trying to fix its [[money problems]] and find new [[investors]]. It says success is not certain.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact or news
verbs.wrong: To post a note for others
verbs.why: Students find out their grades online. Most people find out the news on their phones. Residents found out from a note that they had about seven hours to leave.

verbs.correct: To leave your home and take your things
verbs.wrong: To clean a room for the next guest
verbs.why: Many young adults move out of their parents' homes at 18. College students move out of the dorms in May. Residents had about seven hours to move out of their cabins.

verbs.correct: To find an answer by thinking
verbs.wrong: To book a cheap hotel room
verbs.why: New students figure out the bus routes in a few days. Families figure out a budget when they have little money. Now many residents must figure out where to live.

mainIdea.s: A ship where people bought or rented cabins to live at sea has stopped its trip around the world in Cambodia. Its owner says fuel became too expensive, so all residents had to leave quickly.
mainIdea.why: Fuel costs went up sharply, and the company said it could not pass on the whole increase. Everyone living on the ship had to get off.

mainIdea.s: A floating home for retirees has stopped in Southeast Asia after the old vessel failed a safety check. Officials there told everyone to leave because the ship was no longer safe to keep sailing.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the company stopped the trip itself because fuel costs went up sharply. Nothing says officials found the ship unsafe.

mainIdea.s: A Florida company is building a second, larger ship for people who want to spend their lives traveling. Buyers can pay one price now and live on the new vessel when it begins sailing in 2029.
mainIdea.why: This is about a ship that stopped in Cambodia, not a new ship. Residents had to get off because fuel costs went up sharply.

lines.text: Did you hear about the cruise ship that people actually live on?
The one that sails around the world for years? I thought those people were [[living the dream]].
They were. But the company just had to [[pull the plug]] in Cambodia. Everyone had to {{get off}}.
Fuel costs {{went up}} so much. For each cabin, fuel went from about 1,800 dollars a month to as much as 8,000.
Couldn't they just make the residents pay more?
The company said it couldn't {{pass on}} the whole increase. People already pay a lot to live there.
Did they try to {{cut back on}} fuel first?
Yes. The ship sailed more slowly and stayed longer in ports. It still wasn't enough to {{make up for}} the costs.
How much warning did the residents get?
They {{found out}} at about 7 in the morning and had to leave by 2.
Seven hours to {{move out}}? What [[a rude awakening]].
And some of them sold their houses or {{gave up}} their homes on land to live on board.
So now they're [[left high and dry]] with nowhere to live.
Pretty much. They have to {{figure out}} their next step in a foreign country.
I really hope they [[land on their feet]].
Me too. The company says it will try to fix its money problems in the next 60 days.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone has the life they always wanted
ex: He works from a beach in Mexico. He's living the dream.

expressions.def: To stop a plan or project, often suddenly
ex: The city pulled the plug on the new stadium.

expressions.def: A sudden and unpleasant surprise about how things really are
ex: The first rent bill was a rude awakening for the new students.

expressions.def: Left alone in a bad situation with no help
ex: The airline canceled the flight and left us high and dry.

expressions.def: To reach a good situation after a hard time
ex: They lost their jobs, but they landed on their feet.
Don't worry about her. People like her always land on their feet.
